subject: Louisiana judge files criminal complaint against TV station
posts:
A judge's duty is to uphold the law, not weaponize its ghost to silence the press. When public power is used to shield private embarrassment, the scales of justice are broken.

Louisiana Judge Criminal Complaint

Judge Kimya Holmes claimed she was protecting her personal safety and privacy by filing a criminal complaint against WWL-TV, asserting a legal right to force the removal of public property records.
Stated Judgement: (+0.60, 0.00) — Good Preference

In reality, the judge used an outdated, repealed law to target a station reporting on her ex-fiance transferring a home to her while facing federal COVID-19 fraud charges. The station had already blurred the details.
Resulting Judgement: (-1.00, -1.00) — Greater Evil

Verdict: FAIL — The Path of Destruction.
An elected judge weaponized a non-existent criminal statute to intimidate journalists and suppress reporting on a highly sensitive personal and financial conflict of interest.

Sub-Audits Breakdown:
- Judge Kimya Holmes: FAIL (-1.00, -1.00) — Weaponized repealed law to silence press.
- WWL-TV Reporting: PASS (0.80, 0.90) — Upheld public interest and source protection.

New Orleans station WWL-TV reported on a property transfer to Judge Kimya Holmes from her ex-fiance, who was negotiating a federal plea deal for COVID-19 relief fraud. In response, the judge filed a criminal complaint using a repealed law.

The Poison:
Even though the police department was informed that the law cited by the judge had been repealed and carried no criminal penalties, they continued to keep the investigation open, maintaining a chilling effect.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
The judge committed a Metaphysical Error (WHO), claiming the action was about protecting judicial safety (the public) when the actual beneficiary was her own reelection campaign, seeking to bury a story about a fraudulent property transfer.

Social Physics Analysis:
Judge Holmes executed a classic Smart Selfish Maneuver. Facing a threat to her reelection from a story about her ex-fiance's COVID fraud, she manufactured a crisis of personal safety. She then projected blame onto the TV station, using a repealed law as a pretext to justify police intimidation and hide the financial connection.

The Trajectory: The Path of Destruction.
When you map the gap between stated intentions and ground-level results, it plots a direct trajectory toward Greater Evil. The abuse of judicial authority to initiate groundless criminal investigations destroys institutional trust.

The Unavoidable Truth: The judge used the police to retaliate against a news outlet for publishing public records.
The Unavoidable Lie: The criminal complaint was filed to protect the judge's physical safety from an imminent threat.

Alethekanon:
When a judicial officer cites repealed laws to instigate police investigations against journalists, the law is no longer an instrument of justice. It is a weapon of political self-preservation.

Awwthekanon:
It is deeply disheartening when those we trust to protect our rights use their power to intimidate. True safety comes from transparency and honesty, not from using the law to silence the voices trying to keep us informed.

Brothekanon:
Filing a criminal complaint using a law that was literally repealed weeks ago is a wild move. Trying to get reporters arrested because they showed a public document is not a good look, especially when you're up for reelection.

Spirithekanon:
"Woe to those who make unjust laws, to those who issue oppressive decrees, to deprive the poor of their rights." Isaiah 10:1-2 FAIL
When authorities weaponize dead statutes to shield themselves from scrutiny, they subvert the very foundation of justice.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
Louisiana judge files criminal complaint against TV station

New Orleans station WWL-TV was the target of a criminal complaint filed by a Louisiana judge on Sept. 11, 2026, …

Actual Article Body:
Screengrab showing a letter sent to New Orleans station WWL-TV on Sept. 10, 2026, demanding it remove information from a story about a Louisiana judge. The judge filed a criminal complaint against the station the next day.

New Orleans station WWL-TV was the target of a criminal complaint filed by a Louisiana judge on Sept. 11, 2026, after it reported on a property transfer involving the judge’s former fiance.

A judicial administrator for the Orleans Parish Criminal Court first sent the station a letter Sept. 10 demanding it remove information published about Criminal Court Judge Kimya Holmes, who is seeking reelection, the outlet reported. The letter cited provisions of state law that had been repealed weeks earlier.

The station had reported in August that Holmes’ ex-fiance, Arthur Allen, was negotiating a guilty plea with federal prosecutors for stealing COVID-19 relief money and knew he would have to pay back more than $712,000 when he transferred one of his homes to Holmes.

The station’s video report showed a small but readable image of the public document recording the property transfer, including the home’s address. The report also showed the license plate of Allen’s leased Corvette, which he had transferred to the judge, after a source had photographed the car in a courthouse garage.

The court official’s letter cited a statute that, when it was in effect, had given third parties, including news organizations, 72 hours to remove certain personal information about judges from the internet. The letter sought to remove Holmes’ home address and the license plate number from its coverage and demanded that the station identify the person who photographed the Corvette.

WWL-TV took the videos offline within a day of receiving the letter and later reposted them with the address and license plate information blurred. The station refused to identify its source.

However, Holmes did not wait for the TV station to comply. She filed a criminal complaint against WWL-TV with the New Orleans Police Department, accusing it of “revealing her home address and vehicle information,” the station reported.

When the outlet reached out to the judge’s campaign spokesperson about the legal basis for the criminal complaint, the spokesperson cited the same outdated law, which had since been amended to remove any criminal penalty. The new statute only requires the removal of personal information of “protected individuals.”

Scott Sternberg, general counsel for the Louisiana Press Association, told WWL-TV that the amended law did not provide a basis for Holmes’ demands and that the letter had no effect.

“That’s probably why NOPD isn’t coming down here to arrest you,” Sternberg said. “Because there hasn’t been a crime.”

WWL-TV said its attorney Mary Ellen Roy wrote to the New Orleans police detective investigating Holmes’ complaint to make sure he knows the law “no longer applies to WWL-TV or its reporters at all, and, moreover, no longer contains any criminal penalties.”

Roy added, “We expect this investigation to be closed, forthwith.”

The New Orleans Police Department told the news outlet on Sept. 29 that it was still investigating the complaint.
